When you disagree with someone, there are two paths forward. The first is to try to engage with what they’re saying: what their reasons are, whether their position is true, what evidence could be brought to bear, and so on. The second is to diagnose them: to engage with the second-order question of why they’re saying it. For instance, if you’re arguing with somebody about microservices1, you could say “well, you only like microservices because you want to polish your resume”, or “you only like monoliths because you’re scared of distributed systems”.

This happens a lot in online arguments. On the question “are AI models improving”, some anti-AI people will argue that people only think so because AI psychosis is rotting their brain, and the dumber they get, the smarter AI models seem in comparison. Likewise, many pro-AI people argue that people only disagree because they’re Luddites, or scared of change, and so on. None of these arguments are about the quality of AI models.

It feels so good to diagnose your opponents because there’s no possible response. If you say “I think AI models are improving because these benchmark scores are rising”, somebody might point out that the AI labs are training on those benchmarks, or argue that they represent isolated skills that don’t transfer, and so on, making you feel stupid. If you say “you only disagree with me because you want to roleplay as a revolutionary”, how could you be proven wrong? The more someone protests a diagnosis, the more it sounds like it must be right. Otherwise why would they be so upset?

Of course, they’re so upset precisely because there is no possible response. By moving to diagnosis, you’re no longer having an argument about the facts, you’re purely in the area of rhetoric. But when you’re in the middle of an argument, diagnosing always feels like you’re being piercingly analytical. It feels like you’re cutting right to the heart of the matter: these complicated arguments are just chaff, intended to distract you from the fundamental psychological reason why your opponent is being so foolish. This is just ordinary spite and anger2, whatever it feels like at the time.

There’s nothing inherently wrong with the second-order question of why someone person believes what they believe. It’s totally fine to think about it or form theories about it, like any other factual question. Just remember that it doesn’t bear on the question of whether they’re right3. Every human being forms their beliefs on top of a cocktail of base urges, animal instincts, and barely-suppressed evolutionary drives. If they’re rational, they also have evidence for those beliefs. It’s the quality of that evidence that helps you determine whether the beliefs are true, not the existence of the base urges.

As a general rule, you should only diagnose your opponents when you also have a strong, unrelated argument about why they’re wrong. For instance, I think Ed Zitron has been thoroughly audience-captured by AI skeptics, whose demand for news about AI failures far exceeds supply. But I have written many long-form posts about why I think Zitron’s specific claims about the sustainability of AI are incorrect. When I talk to people who think Zitron is right, I talk about my arguments in those posts, not about my personal theory about why he says the things he does.

Scott Alexander famously called the “noncentral fallacy”4 the Worst Argument in the World. For me, diagnosing your opponents is the Worst Argument in the World. I cringe every time I see it in the wild (like most cringeworthy behavior, it bothers me because I myself have to struggle against the urge to do it). Just don’t! It’s good at playing to your base, but it doesn’t persuade: anyone who believes your opponents’ views will just be mad that you’re psychoanalyzing them instead of talking about the actual issues at stake.

Don’t.
↩

Am I diagnosing the diagnosers here? Maybe, but I think it’s forgivable, since there is no specific argument about the facts at stake.
↩

The philosopher in me wants to clarify that you could theoretically establish that someone’s motives for believing something are leading them away from the truth. In practice, (a) you cannot do this in an internet argument, and (b) it is always better and easier to make a straightforward argument about what the truth is.
↩

“You’re a fringe member of some group which has members I have an emotional reaction to, therefore I will have the same reaction to you even though you yourself don’t do those things.” “Group” here is to be understood as “Christian” or “Italian”, not something like the WBC where the fact of membership itself is what’s being judged.

Selling outIn 1973, Tom Lehrer famously sang that “selling out is easy to do”. That may have been true in the seventies, but it’s not true today: selling out requires both technical skill and a careful sense of how large organizations work in practice. One of the goals of this blog is to teach people how to do it.If you want to live with uncompromised integrity, you don’t need anyone to tell you how: simply always do exactly and only what you want to do. You will be repeatedly punished for it — your managers will dislike you, you will lose jobs and lose out on the chance of getting hired, your financial situation will be less stable, and so on — but that’s just part of the deal. Like deadlifting four plates, it’s not easy, but it is straightforward.Continue reading...

blocks.text: Thursday October 8, 2026 1:17 pm PDT by Joe Rossignol

Starting today, iPhone users still running iOS 26 will see iOS 27.0.1 as the prominent software update in the Settings app under General → Software Update, with iOS 26.7.1 now relegated to a smaller "Also Available" section at the bottom.

iOS 27 was released on September 14, but until now that update and later iOS 27.0.1 were shown under the "Also Available" section, with iOS 26.7 and later iOS 26.7.1 shown in the prominent position. By reversing the order in which the updates are shown today, Apple is more actively encouraging iPhone users who are still on iOS 26 to install iOS 27.
Apple is not forcing iPhone users to install iOS 27, but at least installing iOS 26.7.1 is recommended in order to receive the latest security fixes.
Apple has yet to share iOS 27 adoption numbers.

blocks.text: For me, boredom is just a signal. It means I've hit a roadblock and my brain is trying to convince me not to go any further. "Give up. This sucks anyway. Why are you still wasting your time on this silly thing?"

That's how I feel when I do things I'm really bad at. I think I'm not good at making YouTube videos. Whenever I think of a subject I find really exciting, I start writing, record a first pass, and then load DaVinci Resolve.

With my current schedule, job, family, and responsibilities, I've found that it takes me a whole week to polish three minutes of video. That means I hear the same material I wrote and recorded over and over until it becomes completely boring. After a few weeks, I lose interest in the subject and have no motivation to finish it.

But I think that's just an excuse I tell myself. I like the videos I've managed to complete. I wish I could change some parts, but I still like the final product. It's just that the process gets in the way, and it does so because I have no expertise in making videos. But then again, I always go back to my trusted method: if you're bad at something, do it at least a hundred times before you decide to give up.

We all suck at the beginning, and we're in no position to judge a craft until we've practiced it enough to love it or hate it. So here's to another attempt. I'll be publishing videos in the coming weeks. The first one will be just a minute long, the second will be two minutes long, the third... you get the gist. Hope you enjoy it.

articles.title: I paid people to try and follow my README
articles.titleZh: I paid people to try and follow my README
articles.summary: I paid people to try and follow my README

blocks.text: Developers suck at writing documentation. We like to say RTFM but often there ain't no FM to R. At best we have a half-arsed collection of notes, some obsolete tips, and a link to a desolate forum full of people asking the same questions again and again. That's no way to treat our users.

I naïvely believe there's a better way. As I've written before, you should sit down and actually test your readme. Spin up a fresh Virtual Machine, go through what you've written, and see if it makes sense.

But it is really hard to ignore your own biases. Of course you know that certain commands require sudo and obviously when you wrote -foo you meant --foo and everyone knows that you have to reboot afterwards.
How do you get rid of those biases? I paid people!

As part of my NLnet grant application for ActivityBot, I said I wanted to test the install experience with real users and I was prepared to pay them €25 for an hour of their time. I stuck out the call on Mastodon, gathered a few people, and had a video call with them.

The format was simple. I explained that I was looking for feedback on the first-run experience. I knew that it wasn't perfect and actively wanted constructive criticism. I asked the volunteer to share their screen and, crucially, to speak aloud. Tell me what they were doing. What they didn't understand, what confused them, what delighted them, what frustrated them, etc.
I took notes by hand (fuck feeding the machine) and spent several hours being told what incorrect assumptions I'd made.
Amongst the highlights I discovered were:
The link to the demo tool was wrong.
Some people read a README in the terminal.
What does it actually mean to rename a file?
How do you rename a hidden file?
Should a demo tool be available on the web or just the user's local machine?
Why does some text explicitly need to be quoted and some not?
My jokes aren't funny and are actively confusing.
Some of the technical terminology needed explaining.
The ordering of the different sections was confusing.
I hadn't actually explained what the software would do.
A whole section which was technically interesting to me was utterly confusing to everyone else.
Not all web servers use permissions in the same way.
And on it went!
After each session I updated the README based on what people found difficult, then I re-tested it with the next person.
In total, I paid out around €150 to have a bunch of people criticise me to my face. Hey, cheaper than therapy, right?

I know someone is going to say "why not just ask an LLM to simulate a range of users?" The answer is very simple - I want to speak to real people. People are brilliant! They can make you laugh, you can see their cat when it wanders on to the call, they bring a unique perspective to the problem, and they're really happy when you give them a €25 voucher. Some will gladly do it for free and make you happy!

When I was doing technical writing for GOV.UK, all my beautiful prose was given a second-eye by another human. They eviscerated all my flowery phrases and turned the document into something more readable. They were the ones who caught the mistakes that no spell chequer could. They were able to have a proper conversation with me. More importantly, I could hear the frustration in their voice - that's the thing which lets you know a mistake needs to be corrected.

I don't claim that ActivityBot's README is now perfect - far from it - but it is now demonstrably easier to follow. Developers need to talk to real people. You don't have to pay them if you can't afford it - but find a few people who will talk aloud while they try to follow your instructions. I guarantee you that your README will become much better for it.

blocks.text: Telecommunications pioneer Ward Christensen was born October 23, 1945 in West Bend, Wis. He died aged 78 October 11, 2024 in Rolling Meadows, Ill., a suburb of Chicago. Christensen invented the Xmodem file transfer protocol and co-invented the bulletin board system, two innovations that greatly increased the utility of modems when used with small computers.
Ward Christensen’s professional career
In 1968, Christensen graduated from Milton College with a Bachelor of Arts in physics and chemistry. Later that same year, IBM hired Christensen as a systems engineer.

He worked for IBM for 44 years, until he retired in 2012. His last job title at IBM was field technical sales specialist. In a 1993 interview, he said he was disappointed to start at IBM and find they didn’t have computers in their sales offices. He said in the same interview he lobbied IBM and other companies to release a small computer in the 1970s, but they didn’t see the market.
IBM did eventually see the market for it and released a small computer in 1981.

For about half of Christensen’s tenure at IBM, it had a policy of full employment. If you did your job and met expectations, you had a job for as long as you wanted it. IBM’s financial troubles in the early 1990s brought an end to that, but Christensen was able to navigate the workforce reductions–IBM didn’t call them that, and they definitely didn’t call them layoffs–and spend his entire career with one company.
Writing in his July 1983 Byte magazine column, Jerry Pournelle called Ward Christensen “a public benefactor.” His job security at IBM allowed him to be one.

Christensen didn’t wait for IBM to get involved with small computers. In 1975, he purchased an Altair computer and joined the Chicago Area Computer Hobbyists’ Exchange. He recounted that the club had a cork bulletin board at meetings that club members used to post notes to one another.

After Hayes released its first modems, Christensen started thinking about the idea of a bulletin board system to facilitate transferring files and messages among club members, an electronic equivalent to the corkboard. In January 1978, during a snowstorm, he worked on the idea with his friend Randy Suess. Christensen wrote the software, while Seuss put together a computer to run it on. Both Suess and Christensen donated parts to the effort. Suess found some surplus parts at a computer store to complete the machine. The board, CBBS, went online in February 1978.
They published an article about it in the November 1978 issue of Byte magazine.

The software to access it already existed. In August 1977, Christensen had released a simple telecommunications program for CP/M called modem.asm that allowed a comptuer and modem to emulate a terminal, and included a file transfer protocol called Xmodem.

Christensen was a prolific developer. In 1983, Jerry Pournelle wrote of a collection of CP/M public domain software that “probably 50 percent of the really good programs were written by Ward Christensen.”

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.
